predictions.explanation: Meta did ship a major AI launch in the predicted 4–6 week window: on July 18, 2023 it announced and released Llama 2, a much more capable successor to its earlier LLaMA models, with weights available, commercial use allowed in many cases, and broad distribution via partners like Microsoft Azure and others. This clearly counts as significantly expanded support for its "open" LLM. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama_%28language_model%29?utm_source=openai)) However, the other key part of the prediction — that Meta would launch "a bunch of" agent-style bots on WhatsApp and Instagram in that same 4–6 week window — did not happen. Meta’s conversational assistant (Meta AI) and the 28 AI characters/personas usable as chatbots across WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram were only introduced publicly at Meta Connect on September 27–28, 2023, with rollout beginning then, roughly 11–12 weeks after the July 9 podcast date, not within 4–6 weeks. ([about.fb.com](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/09/introducing-ai-powered-assistants-characters-and-creative-tools/amp/?utm_source=openai)) Because the prediction was conjunctive (major AI launches including both expanded support for the open LLM and the near-term launch of multiple agents on WhatsApp and Instagram) and the agent/bot launches clearly missed the specified time frame, the overall prediction did not come true as stated.

Available user-milestone data for Threads shows that it did **not** reach 100 million registered users within roughly 24 hours of launch.

Key points:
- Threads launched late on **July 5, 2023** (July 5 in the Americas, July 6 elsewhere).([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/07/10/instagrams-threads-app-reaches-100-million-users-in-just-five-days/?utm_source=openai))
- By the **morning of July 6**, Mark Zuckerberg reported about **30 million sign‑ups** – well short of 100 million.([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/07/05/threads-passes-2-million-downloads-in-2-hours/?utm_source=openai))
- By **July 7**, sign‑ups had risen to around **70 million**.([time.com](https://time.com/6292957/threads-fastest-growing-apps/?utm_source=openai))
- Multiple independent tallies (Quiver Quantitative, widely reported in tech and business press) show Threads crossing **100 million sign‑ups around July 10, 2023**, about **five days after launch**, not within the first day.([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/07/10/instagrams-threads-app-reaches-100-million-users-in-just-five-days/?utm_source=openai))

Since all consistent public data indicates the 100M milestone was reached several days after launch—not by the end of the day following launch—the prediction that Threads would hit **100 million registered users within ~24 hours** is **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
Chamath’s claim (July 2023) was that the *“real stuff”* in AI for **enterprise software, healthcare, and the physical sciences** was still *18–24 to 36 months away* from becoming **“real products that actually work.”** That implies such products would not meaningfully appear before roughly **January 2025**.

In practice, all three areas saw substantial, working products **well before** 18 months had elapsed:

- **Enterprise software:**
  - **Microsoft 365 Copilot** became generally available to enterprise customers on **November 1, 2023** (about 4 months after the podcast), with tens of thousands of enterprise users in the early access program, and then was expanded to organizations of all sizes via CSP and other channels in **January 2024**, explicitly marketed as an AI assistant embedded across Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams, etc.([microsoft.com](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/blog/2023/09/21/announcing-microsoft-365-copilot-general-availability-and-microsoft-365-chat/?msockid=18b9727aeb16638204ed6416ea456268&utm_source=openai))  These are large-scale, paid, production deployments in core enterprise workflows, not speculative demos.
  - **Salesforce Einstein Copilot** reached general availability in **April 2024**, with customers like ADP using it to automate processes and enhance productivity via conversational AI grounded in enterprise data.([salesforce.com](https://www.salesforce.com/news/press-releases/2024/04/25/einstein-copilot-general-availability/?utm_source=openai))  Again, this is a live, commercial product integrated into a major enterprise platform.

- **Healthcare:**
  - By **January 2023** (months *before* the prediction), the FDA had already cleared **over 520 AI medical algorithms**, mostly for imaging.([pathologynews.com](https://www.pathologynews.com/computational-pathology-ai/fda-has-now-cleared-more-than-500-healthcare-ai-algorithms-four-of-which-are-for-pathology?utm_source=openai))  By **August 2024**, that number had risen to **about 950 cleared AI/ML-enabled medical products**, with radiology alone accounting for 723 algorithms.([healthimaging.com](https://healthimaging.com/topics/healthcare-management/healthcare-policy/fda-adds-dozens-ai-enabled-radiology-applications-list-clearances?utm_source=openai))  These are regulated clinical products in routine use, not future concepts.
  - **Nuance DAX Copilot**, an ambient, generative‑AI assistant that automatically drafts clinical notes during patient visits and is **embedded in Epic and other EHRs**, was already deployed at **55+ healthcare organizations** and scaling to many more by **March 2024**.([news.nuance.com](https://news.nuance.com/2024-03-07-WellSpan-Health-Advances-Its-Leadership-in-Delivering-Exceptional-Provider-and-Patient-Experience-with-Nuance-DAX-Copilot?utm_source=openai))  Large systems (e.g., Northwestern Medicine) rolled it out enterprise‑wide to reduce documentation burden and physician burnout—clear, production, value‑delivering use.

- **Physical sciences / R&D:**
  - In **November 2023**, Google DeepMind’s **GNoME** system used deep learning to predict **2.2 million new crystal structures**, including about **380,000 stable materials**, an expansion likened to ~800 years’ worth of materials discoveries.([deepmind.google](https://deepmind.google/en/blog/millions-of-new-materials-discovered-with-deep-learning/?utm_source=openai))  These predictions were integrated into resources like the Materials Project and used to drive autonomous labs that successfully synthesized dozens of new compounds, showing immediate scientific utility.
  - **Isomorphic Labs** (an Alphabet/DeepMind spin‑out) signed multi‑billion‑dollar strategic drug‑discovery partnerships with **Eli Lilly and Novartis** in **January 2024** to apply its AI platform to real drug pipelines,([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2024/01/07/isomorphic-inks-deals-with-eli-lilly-and-novartis-for-drug-discovery/?utm_source=openai)) and by **2025** reported it was *“very close”* to starting human trials of AI‑designed drugs.([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/technology/tech-news/google-deepmind-is-ready-to-start-human-trials-of-ai-designed-drugs-company-exec-says-were-getting-very-close/articleshow/122282344.cms?utm_source=openai))  These are concrete, productized applications in pharmaceutical R&D, not distant lab curiosities.

By **mid‑2024**—between **4 and 12 months** after the podcast—there were already:
- Widely sold and deployed **enterprise copilots** embedded in core productivity and CRM suites.
- Hundreds of **regulated, clinically used AI tools** plus rapidly scaling generative‑AI documentation copilots in major health systems.
- Operational AI systems in **materials discovery and drug design** that industry and labs were actively using.

So while Chamath was directionally right that these domains would become major centers of AI progress, his **timing**—“still 18–24 to 36 months away from seeing the light of day as real products that actually work”—was too conservative. Substantive, working, and widely deployed AI products in all three categories were already in place **well before** his 18‑month lower bound, making the prediction **wrong on its stated timeframe**, even though the general thesis about where value would emerge has proved accurate.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence broadly matches the *first* part of Brad Gerstner’s prediction (a fall 2023 rebound) but clearly contradicts the *second* part (stabilizing around 100–150M users).

1. **Fall 2023 usage did rebound after the summer dip.**
   * Similarweb-based estimates show ChatGPT web visits peaking around **1.8B** in April 2023, then falling to **1.6B (June)**, **1.5B (July)** and **1.4B (August)**, before rising again to **1.5B in September** and **1.7B in October 2023**, consistent with a back‑to‑school uptick after the summer slowdown. ([aiprm.com](https://www.aiprm.com/chatgpt-statistics/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Summaries of Reuters/Similarweb coverage note that traffic fell from 1.8B visits to 1.43B by August 2023, then increased once schools returned in September, explicitly attributing the rebound to school being back in session. ([notta.ai](https://www.notta.ai/en/blog/chatgpt-statistics/?utm_source=openai))  
   * So the **"kids come back to school, you’re going to see the normal uptick in traffic"** portion of the prediction is supported by observed data.

2. **However, usage did *not* merely “hang out” around 100–150M users; it grew far beyond that.**
   * Multiple compiled stats (drawing on Axios/Reuters/TechCrunch) put ChatGPT at about **50M weekly active users in January 2023** and **~100M weekly active users by August 2023**. ([twinstrata.com](https://www.twinstrata.com/chatgpt-statistics/?utm_source=openai))  
   * OpenAI CEO Sam Altman publicly stated on **November 6, 2023** that ChatGPT had **100 million weekly active users**, consistent with Gerstner’s “~100M” level in late 2023. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/11/06/openais-chatgpt-now-has-100-million-weekly-active-users/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Other datasets estimate around **150M active users by September 2023**, again within his 100–150M range. ([businessofapps.com](https://www.businessofapps.com/data/chatgpt-statistics/?utm_source=openai))  
   * But after that, usage did *not* stay in that band. Aggregated timelines show:
     * **200M weekly active users by August 2024**  
     * **250–300M weekly active users by late 2024**  
     * **400M weekly active users by February 2025**  
     * **~700–800M weekly active users by mid–late 2025**  
     These figures come from OpenAI statements and secondary analyses (Reuters, Forbes, DemandSage, etc.). ([whop.com](https://whop.com/blog/chatgpt-statistics/?utm_source=openai))

3. **Assessment of the full prediction.**
   * Gerstner’s **directional short‑term call**—that traffic would rebound with back‑to‑school rather than keep sliding—was correct.
   * His **quantitative stabilization call**—that usage would then “hang out” around **100–150M** users instead of moving far above that band—was clearly invalidated within about a year, as weekly and total active users climbed several multiples higher.

Given that the prediction explicitly tied the post‑fall trajectory to a roughly **100–150M user plateau**, and actual usage rapidly exceeded that range rather than stabilizing there, the overall prediction is best classified as **wrong** despite getting the immediate fall 2023 rebound directionally right.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction was that, in the ongoing Bank of England (BoE) tightening cycle as of July 2023, the UK policy rate would *“definitely”* reach 7% and might go to 8%.

What actually happened:

- The BoE’s Bank Rate was raised from 0.1% (December 2021) to a peak of **5.25% in August 2023**, then stopped rising. An official UK Parliament briefing describes the *previous cycle of rate increases* as going from **0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023**, clearly identifying that as the peak of the tightening phase. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/sn02802/?utm_source=openai))
- Historical rate data (BoE/market data series) likewise show **5.25% on 3 August 2023** as the highest level reached, with no subsequent increases beyond that. ([ycharts.com](https://ycharts.com/indicators/bank_of_england_bank_rate?utm_source=openai))
- From August 2024 onward, the BoE began an **easing cycle**, cutting the Bank Rate from 5.25% down to 5.0%, then 4.75%, 4.5%, 4.25%, and eventually **4.0% by August 7, 2025**, confirming that the hiking cycle ended well below 7%. ([marketwatch.com](https://www.marketwatch.com/story/bank-of-england-on-course-for-slowest-ever-pace-of-rate-cuts-but-without-the-abuse-9e323573?utm_source=openai))

Since the tightening cycle referenced in July 2023 peaked at 5.25% and then reversed into cuts, the UK policy rate never reached 7% or 8%. Therefore, Chamath Palihapitiya’s prediction about this cycle’s terminal rate was **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
• The Fed’s last rate hike of the cycle was in July 2023, when it raised the federal funds target to 5.25%–5.50%.([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/interest-rate-cut-decision-federal-reserve-july-september-meeting-2024/?utm_source=openai))  The first *subsequent* rate cut came in September 2024, when the Fed lowered the target range by 0.50 percentage points to 4.75%–5.00%, which mainstream coverage described as the first reduction in four years and the start of an easing phase.([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/fed-rate-cut-decision-federal-reserve-interest-rates-september-meeting/?utm_source=openai))  

• The prediction requires that **before that first cut in September 2024** the U.S. federal government would roll out a new, TARP‑like structured lending or support program specifically aimed at monetizing or backstopping distressed commercial real estate (CRE) debt.

• The only major new crisis‑era lending facility in this period was the **Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP)**, created on March 12, 2023, to provide one‑year loans to banks against Treasuries and agency mortgage‑backed securities valued at par, as a response to the 2023 banking crisis.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Term_Funding_Program?utm_source=openai))  BTFP:
  - predates the July 2023 stance and the podcast;
  - is a general bank‑liquidity backstop, not CRE‑specific; and
  - is not structured as a TARP‑style program to buy or guarantee distressed CRE loans.

• Throughout 2023–2024, top regulators repeatedly flagged commercial real estate as a leading financial‑stability risk but discussed supervisory and market‑based responses, not a federal asset‑purchase or guarantee facility for CRE debt.([facilitiesdive.com](https://www.facilitiesdive.com/news/us-regulators-flag-commercial-real-estate-leading-risk-2024-Fed-SEC/703084/?utm_source=openai))  Coverage of regional banks’ efforts to shed CRE exposure in 2024 similarly describes loan sales, risk‑transfer deals, and "extend‑and‑pretend" restructurings—*again with no mention* of a federal TARP‑like CRE backstop.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/hawkish-fed-impedes-regional-banks-efforts-shed-cre-risks-2024-02-27/?utm_source=openai))

• A TARP‑style program targeted at distressed commercial real estate would be a major policy move and would show up clearly in Fed/Treasury releases and mainstream financial reporting. Extensive searching of 2023–2025 sources turns up only earlier‑era programs (TARP, TALF, 2020 pandemic facilities) and the broad‑based BTFP—not any new CRE‑specific bailout or structured lending program before or around the September 2024 rate cut.

Because the Fed’s first rate cut of this cycle occurred in September 2024 and no such new TARP‑like, CRE‑specific federal support program was rolled out before that date (or since), Friedberg’s prediction did **not** come true.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence shows both key parts of the prediction failed:

1. **Path and peak of the effective fed funds rate in 2023**  
   * The effective fed funds rate was about **5.08% in June 2023**, per monthly data (5.08% for June 2023).([ycharts.com](https://ycharts.com/indicators/effective_federal_funds_rate_monthly?utm_source=openai))  
   * After the Fed’s July 26, 2023 hike to a **5.25–5.50% target range**, the daily effective rate settled around **5.33%** and stayed there through **October and November 2023**; it did **not** rise to ~5.45%.([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/07/26/fed-meeting-july-2023-.html?utm_source=openai))  
   * So the rate did move up from ~5.08%, but it **peaked around 5.33%, not ~5.45%, and that plateau was reached by late summer, not specifically “peaking” in November.**

2. **Timing of the first Fed rate cut**  
   * The Fed kept the **5.25–5.50% target range** unchanged at its December 13, 2023 meeting and explicitly directed operations to maintain that range.([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20231213.htm?utm_source=openai))  
   * It then held the same range again at the January 31, 2024 and subsequent early‑2024 meetings, repeatedly stating it was *not yet* ready to cut.([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2024/jan/31/fed-interest-rates-decision?utm_source=openai))  
   * The **first actual rate cut of this cycle** came on **September 18, 2024**, when the FOMC lowered the target range from **5.25–5.50% to 4.75–5.00%**, reflected in both news reports and the drop in the effective rate from about 5.33% to about 4.83% on September 19, 2024.([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/economy/article/2024/09/19/fed-announces-first-major-rate-cut-since-covid-19-pandemic_6726623_19.html?utm_source=openai))  
   * Thus, there was **no cut between December 2023 and the end of Q1 2024** as predicted; the first cut arrived roughly **six months later** than the latest date in the prediction window.

Because the effective fed funds rate **never reached the forecast peak (~5.45%)** and the **first rate cut occurred well after the predicted Dec‑2023–Q1‑2024 window**, the prediction is best classified as **wrong**.

No further hikes occurred. Critically, no rate cuts happened between December 2023 and Q1 2024; the first cut was September 18, 2024 (50bps to 4.75-5.00%), confirmed by [Federal Reserve](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20240918a.htm), [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/09/18/fed-cuts-rates-september-2024-.html), and others. Rates held steady at 5.25-5.50% target until then ([Bankrate](https://www.bankrate.com/banking/federal-reserve/history-of-federal-funds-rate/), Wikipedia FOMC history).

predictions.explanation:
Chamath’s prediction was made on July 9, 2023, in All-In Podcast E136, where he said: “in the next five to six years, five to ten years, we’re not going to be talking about China the same way we are today.”([podscripts.co](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/all-in-with-chamath-jason-sacks-friedberg/e136-hacking-the-pod-threads-launches-fed-minutes-immigration-debate-balloon-farce-heart-health?utm_source=openai)) This explicitly sets a resolution window of roughly July 2028–July 2033.

As of the current date (November 30, 2025), we are only a bit more than two years into that 5–10 year window. The earliest point at which the prediction could be fairly evaluated (around mid‑2028) has not yet arrived, so it is too early to determine whether U.S. discourse will, by then, have become notably less focused on China as a central adversarial threat.

Current indicators actually show that U.S. political and strategic rhetoric remains strongly centered on China as a primary competitor and security challenge—for example:
- Official U.S. defense strategy documents and commissions continue to describe China as the “pacing challenge” and the preeminent military and strategic threat.([debateus.org](https://debateus.org/hegemony-daily/?utm_source=openai))
- Congress maintains a dedicated House Select Committee on Strategic Competition with the Chinese Communist Party, created in 2023 and still active, whose purpose is explicitly to address economic, technological, and security competition with China.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Select_Committee_on_Strategic_Competition_between_the_United_States_and_the_Chinese_Communist_Party?utm_source=openai))
- Analyses of U.S.–China relations characterize U.S. policy since 2017 as a sustained, comprehensive strategy of strategic competition with China that has persisted across administrations.([china-cee.eu](https://china-cee.eu/2024/05/27/sino-us-relations-and-the-united-states-comprehensive-competition-strategy-against-china/?utm_source=openai))
- Public opinion polling in 2024 shows U.S. views of China at historically high unfavorable levels, reflecting an entrenched adversarial perception.([csis.org](https://www.csis.org/analysis/advancing-us-china-coordination-amid-strategic-competition-emerging-playbook?utm_source=openai))

These facts suggest that, so far, U.S. discourse has *not* shifted in the way Chamath anticipated; if anything, China remains framed as a core rival. However, because the prediction is specifically about conditions **5–10 years** after mid‑2023, and we have not yet reached even the start of that evaluation window, the correct judgment at this time is **“inconclusive” (too early to tell).**

Recent sources confirm ongoing hawkish rhetoric: ITIF report (Nov 17, 2025) warns of China's 'strategic threat' needing new U.S. strategy [https://itif.org/publications/2025/11/17/us-national-power-industries-are-in-deep-jeopardy-washington-needs-new-strategy-to-counter-china-s-strategic-threat-new-report-warns/]; Pew Research (Apr 2025) shows persistent views of China as top threat [https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2025/04/17/views-of-china-as-a-competitor-and-threat-to-the-us/]; congressional bipartisanship on hawkish China stance (Oct 2025) [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/polp.70082].
